features.name: Academic attainment
features.description: The applicant's level of formal academic preparation in computer science or a related technical field.

levels.descriptor: Bachelor's degree or equivalent practical experience only, with no advanced degree presented.
Master's degree in computer science or a related field is presented.
Doctoral degree in computer science or a related field is presented.

features.name: Agentic systems design
features.description: Direct experience designing or owning agent-based systems, including their orchestration, control boundaries, and guardrails.

levels.descriptor: No agent-based systems experience described.
Mentions agents or agentic workflows without architecture detail.
Describes building agentic tooling with a clear split between agents and supporting services.
Shows deliberate design of bounded, auditable, constrained agent systems with explicit guardrails and backend control.

features.name: Algorithmic fluency
features.description: Practical command of data structures and algorithms as demonstrated through concrete engineering improvements.

levels.descriptor: No algorithmic strength is mentioned.
Algorithmic fluency is claimed, but without a concrete example.
At least one specific redesign or optimization shows applied algorithmic thinking.
Multiple or especially vivid examples show data structures and algorithms materially shaping system design.

features.name: Applied AI production experience
features.description: Hands-on experience shipping AI or LLM functionality in production and treating it as an operational reliability problem rather than mere novelty.

levels.descriptor: No AI evidence.
Only vague, aspirational, or lightly specified AI mention.
Shows concrete experience shipping AI or LLM-backed functionality.
Shows concrete production AI work plus explicit evaluation, guardrails, correctness, or failure-mode management.

features.name: Developer enablement mindset
features.description: Whether the applicant frames security engineering as helping developers do the right thing through defaults, tooling, and reduced friction.

levels.descriptor: No developer-centered security philosophy is visible.
Shows generic interest in improving security but not specifically in making life easier for developers.
Explicitly talks about secure-by-default workflows, reducing friction, or helping teams do the right thing.
Strongly frames security as developer enablement, emphasizing defaults, tools, or guardrails over policing, process, or documents.

features.name: Engineering rigor
features.description: The extent to which the letter emphasizes correctness, testing, discipline, guardrails, and dependable engineering standards for security-sensitive software.

levels.descriptor: Provides little evidence of maintainability, testing, safety, or operational care.
Shows some signals of care, such as a maintainer mindset or concern for correctness, but not many concrete practices.
Names explicit rigor practices such as testing, typing, bounded actions, release discipline, or failure recovery.
Repeatedly signals high production standards and a habit of building dependable systems with strong constraints and maintainability.

features.name: Evidence specificity
features.description: How consistently the letter substantiates claims with concrete examples, mechanisms, scope, or implementation detail rather than generic assertions.

levels.descriptor: Mostly lists qualities or interests with little supporting evidence.
Includes a few examples but limited detail on ownership or effect.
Gives concrete examples of work with enough detail to make the claims credible.
Repeatedly ties claims to specific actions and clear outcomes or impact.

features.name: Go depth
features.description: How central and substantial Go appears in the applicant's real professional backend work.

levels.descriptor: Go is missing, unclear, or only incidental.
Go is mentioned as a language used, but not as a main vehicle for work.
Go is clearly presented as the primary or day-to-day language.
Go is central to multiple production systems or explicitly tied to backend or security-infrastructure ownership.

features.name: Impact articulation
features.description: How clearly the letter states the practical outcomes or effects of the applicant's work rather than only listing responsibilities.

levels.descriptor: Lists responsibilities or technologies without explaining what changed because of the work.
Suggests benefit, but the outcome remains vague or implied.
Gives a clear before-and-after or operational result, such as a queue becoming routed, a bottleneck disappearing, or hours being saved.
Shows strong leverage-oriented impact articulation, tying the work to measurable capacity, broad downstream benefit, or a transformed operating model.

features.name: Maintainability mindset
features.description: Whether the applicant explicitly values long-term operability, inheritance, maintenance, and durability of systems.

levels.descriptor: Shows no explicit maintainability or reliability orientation.
Implies care for quality but not as a recurring theme.
Clearly values maintainable, dependable systems or draws on maintenance experience.
Makes long-term operability a central lens, emphasizing inheritance, quiet resilience, or higher standards for security-critical software.

features.name: Narrative coherence
features.description: Whether the letter reads as a well-structured, coherent story or argument linking background, motivation, and fit.

levels.descriptor: The letter reads like disconnected bullets, fragments, or stacked claims.
The letter has some structure, but transitions or the overall arc are uneven.
The letter coherently links background, technical experience, and interest in the role.
The letter presents an especially well-shaped narrative that makes the applicant's trajectory and fit feel natural.

features.name: Narrative distinctiveness
features.description: Whether the letter has a memorable, individualized voice or thesis rather than sounding generic or templated.

levels.descriptor: Highly formulaic prose with little individual voice.
Competent but generic prose with only limited individuality.
Includes a memorable framing device, belief, or personal thesis.
Sustains a distinctive, authentic voice throughout while still serving the application's purpose.

features.name: Offensive security practice
features.description: Ongoing attacker-oriented practice outside ordinary product engineering, such as CTFs or similar offensive exercises.

levels.descriptor: No offensive-security practice is mentioned.
Shows occasional or casual participation in CTFs or similar practice.
Shows sustained participation in CTFs or other regular adversarial practice.
Shows sustained adversarial practice with strong competitive results or clearly serious investment.

features.name: Open-source stewardship
features.description: Public engineering contribution or maintenance responsibility beyond the applicant's employer codebase.

levels.descriptor: No open-source contribution or maintenance described.
Mentions occasional upstream patches or light contribution.
Shows active contribution or maintenance with review or release responsibility.
Maintains a used project or framework with sustained community, release, review, or user-support responsibilities.

features.name: Personal project ambition
features.description: The technical ambition and seriousness of self-directed engineering work outside formal employment.

levels.descriptor: No personal project is mentioned.
Mentions a small utility or light side project with modest technical scope.
Describes a substantive side project with meaningful systems or infrastructure work.
Describes an ambitious self-directed systems project tackling distributed correctness, recovery, delivery guarantees, or similarly hard engineering problems.

features.name: Platform leverage orientation
features.description: Motivation toward foundational infrastructure or shared tooling whose benefits compound across many teams.

levels.descriptor: Does not mention foundational leverage or broader organizational impact.
Expresses a general desire for scale or impact but without a clear platform orientation.
Explicitly wants infrastructure or foundational work that benefits many teams.
Repeatedly frames motivation around downstream leverage, central-platform responsibility, or quiet improvements inherited across an organization.

features.name: Production software track record
features.description: The applicant's accumulated relevant professional experience building, shipping, maintaining, and operating production software systems.

levels.descriptor: Meets the baseline only, with limited scope or a small number of launched systems described.
Shows a solid early-career record, with several years and some repeated launch or maintenance work.
Shows a strong mid-career record, with multiple launches and clear production breadth.
Presents an extensive record for this role, combining years, repeated launches, and broad responsibility across production systems.

features.name: Python depth
features.description: How deeply and credibly the letter presents Python as a serious production language for services, tooling, automation, or agents.

levels.descriptor: No Python experience is mentioned.
Mentions Python briefly or only as light scripting.
Describes regular Python use for tooling, automation, or services.
Shows deep Python ownership across production services or critical internal tooling.

features.name: Role-specific fit
features.description: How specifically the letter explains interest in this exact role and maps the applicant's background to the posting's stated requirements or responsibilities.

levels.descriptor: The fit is vague and the reader must infer most of the relevance.
Some relevant matches are stated, but the mapping to the posting is incomplete or indirect.
Clearly connects several experiences to the role's stated needs.
Makes the match easy to verify, systematically covering most of the key qualifications or responsibilities.

features.name: Security assessment practice
features.description: Hands-on experience evaluating systems for security weaknesses and following findings through validation or remediation.

levels.descriptor: No security assessment work is mentioned.
Mentions security reviews or assessments only in general terms.
Describes concrete assessment work such as threat models, design reviews, or attack-surface analysis.
Shows repeated, substantive assessment work with follow-through such as documented findings, remediation validation, or attacker-style code reading.

features.name: Security automation mission insight
features.description: Understanding of the role's core mission as leverage-heavy security automation that scales scarce expertise and changes behavior at organizational scale.

levels.descriptor: Shows little role-specific framing beyond wanting security impact.
Shows general interest in secure defaults or automation, but not a sharp view of the problem.
Clearly frames security tooling as a way to scale review, response, or manual workload.
Frames the problem sharply in terms of scarce expert attention, organization-wide signal handling, variant analysis, or systems-level leverage.

features.name: Security collaboration mindset
features.description: Whether the applicant emphasizes partnering with security specialists and serving internal users rather than presenting the work as purely solo implementation.

levels.descriptor: Does not signal collaboration with security specialists or users of the tooling.
Uses general teamwork or internal-customer language, but without much specificity.
Explicitly wants to work closely with security engineers, learn from domain specialists, or build in tight proximity to the teams served.

features.name: Security credential strength
features.description: The presence and rigor of formal external credentials used to validate the applicant's security knowledge or hands-on skill.

levels.descriptor: No relevant security certification is stated.
A baseline or survey credential such as Security+ is stated.
A rigorous hands-on credential such as OSCP or a similarly demanding practical certification is stated.

features.name: Security philosophy
features.description: Whether the letter articulates a thoughtful security-engineering worldview or presents the applicant as already thinking and operating like a security engineer.

levels.descriptor: Little sign of a security-specific philosophy or perspective.
Expresses seriousness about security, but only in generic terms.
Shows a clear personal lens such as attacker thinking, builder's-eye reviewing, or preference for quiet resilience.
Presents a memorable, role-relevant philosophy that convincingly shapes how the applicant builds and evaluates systems.

features.name: Vulnerability triage automation
features.description: Experience building software that automates intake, classification, routing, deduplication, or related handling of vulnerability reports.

levels.descriptor: No vulnerability handling automation is mentioned.
Security automation is mentioned, but the triage workflow itself remains vague.
The letter clearly shows experience automating vulnerability intake, routing, or triage.
The letter describes a high-resolution triage pipeline with elements like classification, deduplication, prioritization, ownership, or clear manual-work reduction.

features.name: Writing polish
features.description: Surface-level professionalism of the letter's spelling, grammar, proofreading, and copy-editing accuracy.

levels.descriptor: Frequent errors, misspellings, or naming mistakes noticeably distract from the application.
Several noticeable errors appear, but the letter remains readable.
Mostly clean writing with only minor slips.
Polished, professional, and essentially error-free throughout.

other.name: Other
other.description: Genuinely distinct or idiosyncratic dimensions that do not clearly share a single underlying construct with a broader recurring group.

levels.descriptor: No security engagement outside day-job claims is shown.
A modest external signal is shown, such as casual CTF participation or a baseline security credential.
A strong external signal is shown, such as serious competitive CTF results or a hands-on credential like OSCP.
Multiple strong external signals are shown, such as both high-level CTF performance and a hands-on offensive certification.
